claim: Coral reefs are some of the most important and ecologically diverse marine environments.
source: Coral reefs are some of the most important and ecologically diverse marine environments.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about coral reef ecosystems.

claim: Dinoflagellate algae live symbiotically within coral cells at the base of the reef ecosystem.
source: At the base of the reef ecosystem are dinoflagellate algae, which live symbiotically within coral cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the symbiotic relationship between dinoflagellates and corals.

claim: The lack of dinoflagellate genetic transformation technology has hampered efforts to understand the alga-coral relationship.
source: Efforts to understand the relationship between alga and coral have been greatly hampered by the lack of an appropriate dinoflagellate genetic transformation technology.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of available research tools.

claim: Novel genetic material has been introduced into the dinoflagellate chloroplast genome using the plasmid-like fragmented chloroplast genome.
source: By making use of the plasmid-like fragmented chloroplast genome, we have introduced novel genetic material into the dinoflagellate chloroplast genome.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including PCR detection and sequencing results.

claim: The introduced genes are expressed and confer the expected phenotypes.
source: We have shown that the introduced genes are expressed and confer the expected phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data showing transcription, immunofluorescence showing protein expression, and survival under selection showing phenotype.

claim: Genetically modified cultures have been maintained for 1 year with subculturing while maintaining the introduced genes and phenotypes.
source: Genetically modified cultures have been grown for 1 year with subculturing, maintaining the introduced genes and phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing long-term culture survival and PCR detection of introduced genes after extended periods.

claim: Cells continue to divide after transformation.
source: This indicates that cells continue to divide after transformation and that the transformation is stable.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cultures survived and were subcultured over extended periods.

claim: The transformation is stable.
source: This indicates that cells continue to divide after transformation and that the transformation is stable.
evidence: This is supported by data showing maintenance of introduced genes and phenotypes over 1 year with subculturing.

claim: This is the first report of stable chloroplast transformation in dinoflagellate algae.
source: This is the first report of stable chloroplast transformation in dinoflagellate algae.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the existing literature and the novelty of the presented results.

claim: Dinoflagellate algae are frequently referred to as zooxanthellae.
source: At the base of the ecosystem are dinoflagellate algae, frequently referred to as zooxanthellae.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the terminology used for symbiotic dinoflagellates.

claim: Dinoflagellate algae provide fixed carbon to the coral host.
source: These single-celled algae live in symbiosis with corals as intracellular photosynthetic symbionts, providing fixed carbon to the host.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the metabolic relationship in coral-dinoflagellate symbiosis.

claim: Loss of the symbiotic alga results in coral bleaching.
source: Loss of the symbiotic alga results in coral bleaching, which is one of the most urgent and worsening worldwide ecological concerns.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the mechanism of coral bleaching.

claim: In 2016, 85% of the Great Barrier Reef was affected by coral bleaching.
source: In 2016, 85% of the Great Barrier Reef was found to be affected by coral bleaching, a significantly higher proportion than had been previously identified (Hughes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hughes et al., 2017.

claim: Change in sea water temperature is recognized as one of the environmental causes of coral bleaching.
source: Change in sea water temperature is recognized as one of the environmental causes of coral bleaching (Spalding and Brown, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spalding and Brown, 2015.

claim: Temperature change likely results in disturbance of photosynthetic electron transfer in the dinoflagellate symbiont and consequent damage.
source: It is likely that this results in disturbance of photosynthetic electron transfer in the dinoflagellate symbiont and consequent damage (Rehman et al., 2016), (Slavov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rehman et al., 2016 and Slavov et al., 2016.

claim: The PsbA (D1) reaction center protein of photosystem II is believed to be an important target of bleaching-related damage.
source: The PsbA (D1) reaction center protein of photosystem II is believed to be an important target of such damage (Warner et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Warner et al., 1999.

claim: Key subunits of photosynthetic electron transfer chain complexes, including the PsbA protein, are encoded in the dinoflagellate chloroplast genome.
source: The key subunits of photosynthetic electron transfer chain complexes, including the PsbA protein, are encoded in the dinoflagellate chloroplast genome (Howe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Howe et al., 2008.

claim: There have been no reports to date of transformation of the dinoflagellate chloroplast genome prior to this study.
source: There have been no reports to date of transformation of the dinoflagellate chloroplast genome, hampering attempts to study the mechanism of bleaching.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the existing literature.

claim: There have been numerous attempts at stable nuclear transformation of dinoflagellates, but none has been clearly successful.
source: There have been numerous attempts at stable nuclear transformation of dinoflagellates, but none has been clearly successful.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the existing literature and subsequent citations discussing failed attempts.

claim: An early report described transformation of Amphidinium sp. and Symbiodinium microadriaticum mediated by silicon carbide whiskers with selection for resistance to hygromycin or G418 and using β-glucuronidase (GUS) as a reporter, appearing to produce transformants after 12 weeks.
source: An early report of the transformation of the dinoflagellates Amphidinium sp. and Symbiodinium microadriaticum mediated by silicon carbide whiskers, with selection for resistance to hygromycin or G418 and using β-glucuronidase (GUS) as a reporter, appeared to produce transformants after 12 weeks (ten Lohuis and Miller, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to ten Lohuis and Miller, 1998.

claim: There are no reports of successful use of the silicon carbide whisker technique since the initial publication.
source: However, there are no reports of successful use of this technique since the initial publication.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the existing literature.

claim: In 2019, experiments on Symbiodinium microadriaticum using biolistics, electroporation and agitation with silicon carbide whiskers failed to introduce a chloramphenicol acetyl transferase (CAT) gene to the nuclear genome.
source: In 2019, a series of experiments on Symbiodinium microadriaticum, using biolistics, electroporation and agitation with silicon carbide whiskers failed to introduce a chloramphenicol acetyl transferase (CAT) gene to the nuclear genome (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claim: Ortiz-Matamoros and co-workers reported transient expression of GFP in Symbiodinium using a plasmid designed for plant transformation introduced by treatment with glass beads and polyethylene glycol, with selection for resistance to the herbicide Basta (gluphosinate).
source: Despite this, Ortiz-Matamoros and co-workers reported transient expression of GFP in Symbiodinium using a plasmid designed for plant transformation introduced by treatment with glass beads and polyethylene glycol, and selection for resistance to the herbicide Basta (gluphosinate) (Ortiz-Matamoros et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ortiz-Matamoros et al., 2015a.

claim: Transformed cells from the Ortiz-Matamoros glass bead study were not capable of cell division.
source: However, transformed cells were not capable of cell division, and no genetic confirmation of transformation was carried out.
evidence: This is based on citation to Ortiz-Matamoros et al., 2015a.

claim: No genetic confirmation of transformation was carried out in the Ortiz-Matamoros glass bead study.
source: However, transformed cells were not capable of cell division, and no genetic confirmation of transformation was carried out.
evidence: This is based on citation to Ortiz-Matamoros et al., 2015a.

claim: Transformation with the same plasmid mobilized by Agrobacterium was reported, although the transformed cells failed to divide.
source: Transformation with the same plasmid mobilized by the plant pathogen Agrobacterium was also reported, although the transformed cells again failed to divide (Ortiz-Matamoros et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ortiz-Matamoros et al., 2015b.

claim: The lack of stable expression of heterologous genes limits the use of transient transformation techniques for functional biochemical studies.
source: The lack of stable expression of heterologous genes limits the use of these techniques for functional biochemical studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of transient expression systems.

claim: The chloroplast genome of dinoflagellate species containing the carotenoid peridinin is typically fragmented, comprising approximately 20 plasmid-like DNA molecules of 2–5 kbp known as 'minicircles'.
source: The chloroplast genome of dinoflagellate species containing the carotenoid peridinin (which is the largest group and includes those forming symbionts with coral) is typically fragmented, comprising approximately 20 plasmid-like DNA molecules of 2–5 kbp known as 'minicircles' (Zhang et al., 1999), (Barbrook et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 1999 and Barbrook et al., 2014.

claim: Each minicircle typically carries a single gene, together with a conserved core region which is assumed to contain the origin of replication as well as the transcriptional start site.
source: Each minicircle typically carries a single gene, together with a conserved core region which is assumed to contain the origin of replication as well as the transcriptional start site (Howe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Howe et al., 2008.

claim: Minicircles have been shown to be localized to the chloroplast using in situ hybridization.
source: These minicircles have been shown to be localized to the chloroplast using in situ hybridization (Owari et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Owari et al., 2014.

claim: Each chloroplast contains multiple copies of each minicircle.
source: Each chloroplast contains multiple copies of each minicircle, although the exact copy number varies according to the growth stage of a culture (Koumandou and Howe, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koumandou and Howe, 2007.

claim: The exact copy number of minicircles varies according to the growth stage of a culture.
source: Each chloroplast contains multiple copies of each minicircle, although the exact copy number varies according to the growth stage of a culture (Koumandou and Howe, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koumandou and Howe, 2007.

claim: Two artificial minicircles were created, both based on the psbA minicircle from Amphidinium carterae.
source: We created two artificial minicircles, both based on the psbA minicircle from the dinoflagellate Amphidinium carterae, as the A. carterae chloroplast genome is the best characterized amongst dinoflagellates (Barbrook et al., 2012; Koumandou et al., 2004; Barbrook et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to Barbrook et al., 2012; Koumandou et al., 2004; Barbrook et al., 2001.

claim: The A. carterae chloroplast genome is the best characterized amongst dinoflagellates.
source: We created two artificial minicircles, both based on the psbA minicircle from the dinoflagellate Amphidinium carterae, as the A. carterae chloroplast genome is the best characterized amongst dinoflagellates (Barbrook et al., 2012; Koumandou et al., 2004; Barbrook et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barbrook et al., 2012; Koumandou et al., 2004; Barbrook et al., 2001.

claim: The psbA gene was replaced with a selectable marker in the artificial minicircles.
source: We replaced the psbA gene with a selectable marker (either a modified version of psbA which confers tolerance to the herbicide atrazine (Hirschberg and McIntosh, 1983), or a gene for chloramphenicol acetyl transferase (CAT), which confers resistance to chloramphenicol), and an E. coli plasmid backbone (to allow propagation in E. coli).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to Hirschberg and McIntosh, 1983.

claim: A modified version of psbA confers tolerance to the herbicide atrazine.
source: We replaced the psbA gene with a selectable marker (either a modified version of psbA which confers tolerance to the herbicide atrazine (Hirschberg and McIntosh, 1983), or a gene for chloramphenicol acetyl transferase (CAT), which confers resistance to chloramphenicol), and an E. coli plasmid backbone (to allow propagation in E. coli).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hirschberg and McIntosh, 1983 and experimental data showing survival under atrazine selection.

claim: The chloramphenicol acetyl transferase (CAT) gene confers resistance to chloramphenicol.
source: We replaced the psbA gene with a selectable marker (either a modified version of psbA which confers tolerance to the herbicide atrazine (Hirschberg and McIntosh, 1983), or a gene for chloramphenicol acetyl transferase (CAT), which confers resistance to chloramphenicol), and an E. coli plasmid backbone (to allow propagation in E. coli).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CAT function and is supported by experimental data showing survival under chloramphenicol selection.

claim: Numerous transformation methods were tested.
source: We tested numerous transformation methods and were able to obtain sucessful introduction of these artificial minicircles into dinoflagellates using particle bombardment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data describing glass bead, electroporation, and biolistic methods.

claim: Successful introduction of artificial minicircles into dinoflagellates was achieved using particle bombardment.
source: We tested numerous transformation methods and were able to obtain sucessful introduction of these artificial minicircles into dinoflagellates using particle bombardment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing PCR detection, transcription, and phenotypic effects.

claim: The presence of the artificial minicircles was detected using PCR and RT-PCR following selection.
source: Following selection, we could detect the presence of the artificial minicircles, and transcripts from them, using PCR and RT-PCR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The product of the introduced chloramphenicol acetyl transferase gene was detected using immunofluorescence microscopy.
source: We were able to detect the product of the introduced chloramphenicol acetyl transferase gene using immunofluorescence microscopy.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cultures under selection continued to divide and maintain the artificial minicircles for at least 1 year.
source: Cultures under selection continued to divide and maintain the artificial minicircles for at least 1 year, indicating that transformation was stable.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing long-term culture maintenance and PCR detection.

claim: The availability of a method for dinoflagellate chloroplast transformation enables a range of studies on the maintenance and expression of this genome and the proteins it encodes.
source: The availability of a method for dinoflagellate chloroplast transformation enables a range of studies on the maintenance and expression of this remarkable genome and the proteins it encodes, such as PsbA.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications based on the demonstrated transformation method.

claim: Tolerance to atrazine in plants can be conferred by a single residue change in the PsbA protein, where a Serine is mutated to a Glycine.
source: Tolerance to atrazine in plants can be conferred by a single residue change in the PsbA protein, where a Serine is mutated to a Glycine (Goloubinoff et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goloubinoff et al., 1984.

claim: The psbA minicircle was cloned into the E. coli vector pGEM-T easy.
source: We therefore cloned the A. carterae psbA minicircle into the E. coli vector pGEM-T easy (Promega) and introduced the necessary mutations into the psbA gene using site-directed mutagenesis, Figure 1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The necessary mutations for atrazine resistance were introduced into the psbA gene using site-directed mutagenesis.
source: We therefore cloned the A. carterae psbA minicircle into the E. coli vector pGEM-T easy (Promega) and introduced the necessary mutations into the psbA gene using site-directed mutagenesis, Figure 1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The pAmpChl artificial minicircle is based on the A. carterae psbA minicircle with the psbA gene excised and replaced by an A. carterae codon-optimized gene encoding chloramphenicol acetyl transferase.
source: The second artificial minicircle, pAmpChl, was designed to confer chloramphenicol resistance. It is also based on the A. carterae psbA minicircle, but the psbA gene was excised and replaced by a A. carterae codon-optimized gene encoding chloramphenicol acetyl transferase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data describing the construct design.

claim: The plasmid backbone of pAmpChl is E. coli pMA.
source: The plasmid backbone is E. coli pMA, Figure 1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1.

claim: Silicon carbide whiskers have been previously reported for stable transformation of dinoflagellates.
source: There has been one previous report of stable transformation of dinoflagellates, using silicon carbide whiskers (ten Lohuis and Miller, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to ten Lohuis and Miller, 1998.

claim: Silicon carbide whiskers are a significant health hazard.
source: Additionally, the whiskers are a significant health hazard, and, in other species, glass bead-mediated transformation has a higher transformation efficiency (Ortiz-Matamoros et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the hazards of silicon carbide whiskers.

claim: In other species, glass bead-mediated transformation has a higher transformation efficiency than silicon carbide whiskers.
source: Additionally, the whiskers are a significant health hazard, and, in other species, glass bead-mediated transformation has a higher transformation efficiency (Ortiz-Matamoros et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ortiz-Matamoros et al., 2018.

claim: There has been one previous report of transient transformation of dinoflagellates with glass beads.
source: There has been one previous report of transient transformation of dinoflagellates with glass beads (Ortiz-Matamoros et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ortiz-Matamoros et al., 2015a.

claim: Attempts to replicate glass bead transformation to obtain stable transformation were unsuccessful.
source: We therefore first sought to replicate this finding, by transforming the A. carterae dinoflagellate chloroplast genome using glass beads. We used the artificial minicircle pAmpPSBA followed by selection with atrazine. The experiment was carried out three times, but no viable cells were seen following selection (i.e. following the addition of atrazine, all cells died at the same time that untransformed cells died).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no survival difference between transformed and untransformed cells.

claim: Polyethylene glycol has been reported to increase glass bead transformation efficiency.
source: Polyethylene glycol has been reported to increase glass bead transformation efficiency.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Addition of polyethylene glycol to glass bead transformation did not result in recovery of stable transformants.
source: We therefore added polyethylene glycol and repeated the transformation (in triplicate). No live cells were recovered following selection, indicating that this method did not give rise to stable transformants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no viable cells after selection.

claim: Many eukaryotic protist species can be transformed using electroporation.
source: Many eukaryotic protist species can be transformed using electroporation, and the Lonza Nucleofector system is used with many hard-to-transfect species.
evidence: This is established knowledge about transformation methods.

claim: The Lonza Nucleofector system is used with many hard-to-transfect species.
source: Many eukaryotic protist species can be transformed using electroporation, and the Lonza Nucleofector system is used with many hard-to-transfect species.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Lonza Nucleofector system.

claim: Perkinsus marinus, a sister group to the dinoflagellates, can be transformed using the Lonza Nucleofector.
source: This includes Perkinsus marinus, a sister group to the dinoflagellates (Burkett and Vasta, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burkett and Vasta, 1997.

claim: Attempts to transfect A. carterae using the Lonza Nucleofector with several settings did not recover any transformants.
source: The artificial minicircle pAmpPSBA was used to attempt to transfect A. carterae using the Lonza Nucleofector with several settings indicated as suitable for protist transformation (X-100, D-023, L-029 and EH 100), each in triplicate. We were never able to recover any transformants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no transformants recovered.

claim: Biolistics has been reliably used to transform the unicellular alga Chlamydomonas for 30 years.
source: We next turned to biolistics, since this has been reliably used to transform the unicellular alga Chlamydomonas for 30 years (Boynton et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boynton et al., 1988.

claim: Nine experiments to introduce pAmpPSBA into A. carterae using biolistic transformation were carried out using a range of rupture disk pressures.
source: Nine experiments to introduce the pAmpPSBA artificial minicircle into A. carterae using biolistic transformation were carried out, using a range of rupture disk pressures.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: In six experiments, A. carterae cells shot with particles carrying pAmpPSBA showed greater mean survival time under selection conditions than untransformed cells.
source: In six experiments, A. carterae cells shot with particles carrying pAmpPSBA showed greater mean survival time under selection conditions than untransformed cells, suggesting successful transformation (Experiments A2, A3, A4, A5, A7 and A8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Experiment A1 was carried out using the lowest pressure rupture disks and showed no difference in survival time between control and experimental cells.
source: The first (Experiment A1) was carried out using the lowest pressure rupture disks. In this experiment, control and experimental cells survived just 13 days, suggesting that cells had not been transformed, perhaps because an insufficient bombardment velocity had been applied.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: In Experiment A9, selection was carried out with 1 µg ml−1 atrazine, below the lethal concentration of 2 µg ml−1, and both test and control cultures survived at least three months.
source: In the second experiment (A9), selection was carried out with 1 µg ml−1 atrazine, below the lethal concentration of 2 µg ml−1. Both test and control cultures survived at least three months, with subculturing occurring at 8-week intervals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Transformation attempts were made with A. carterae using chloramphenicol resistance as selectable marker with 1550 p.s.i. rupture disks.
source: Transformation attempts were also made with A. carterae using chloramphenicol resistance as selectable marker. Experiments were carried out with pAmpChl and 1550 p.s.i. rupture disks.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: In Experiment C1A, chloramphenicol was applied after 3 days in liquid culture to allow time for initial synthesis of chloramphenicol acetyl transferase.
source: In the first experiment, chloramphenicol (final concentration 10–50 µg ml−1) was applied after 3 days in liquid culture, to allow time for initial synthesis of chloramphenicol acetyl transferase (Experiments C1A-E), Table 2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: No untransformed wild-type cells survived after 15 days at any chloramphenicol concentration tested in Experiment C1.
source: No untransformed wild-type cells (i.e. shot with gold particles without DNA) survived after 15 days, whatever the chloramphenicol concentration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: At 10 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol, cells shot with particles carrying the pAmpChl plasmid survived for at least 35 days in Experiment C1A.
source: However, at 10 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol, cells shot with particles carrying the pAmpChl plasmid survived for at least 35 days, Experiment C1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: When chloramphenicol concentration was 30 µg ml−1 or greater, cells shot with particles containing the pAmpChl plasmid had died by day 15 in Experiment C1.
source: When chloramphenicol concentration was 30 µg ml−1 or greater, cells shot with particles containing the pAmpChl plasmid had died by day 15, (Experiment C1C-E), Table 2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: DNA was isolated from atrazine-selected A. carterae cultures from experiment A5 (two lines designated A5.1 and A5.2) by vortexing with glass beads.
source: To test if the transformation construct could be recovered from putatively transformed cultures, DNA was isolated from atrazine-selected A. carterae cultures (experiment A5, two lines designated A5.1 and A5.2) by vortexing with glass beads.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: PCR using primers MC-pG-F and MC-pG-R amplified a single product from lines A5.1 and A5.2, with no product detected from wild type or unbroken cells.
source: PCR was performed using the primers MC-pG-F and MC-pG-R (Figure 1) which lie on either side of the junction between the psbA minicircle and the pGEM-T Easy vector. A single product was amplified from each of lines A5.1 and A5.2, with no product detected from either the wild type or the 'unbroken cells' (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The PCR product from lines A5.1 and A5.2 matched the size of product from the positive control.
source: This product matched the size of product from the positive control.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Sequencing confirmed that products from both lines A5.1 and A5.2 were as expected from pAmpPSBA, as a chimaera between the psbA minicircle and the pGEM-T Easy vector.
source: Products from both lines were cloned and sequenced. The sequence was as expected from pAmpPSBA, as a chimaera between the psbA minicircle and the pGEM-T Easy vector, confirming that the atrazine-resistant A. carterae did indeed contain the pAmpPSBA sequence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from DNA sequencing.

claim: DNA was isolated from three chloramphenicol-selected A. carterae lines (C1A.1, C1A.2 and C1A.3) after 35 days of selection.
source: To test if the pAmpChl artificial minicircle was present, DNA was isolated from three chloramphenicol-selected A. carterae lines (C1A.1, C1A.2 and C1A.3) after 35 days of selection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: PCR using primers CAT-F and CAT-R obtained a single product from lines C1A.1 and C1A.3, with no product detected from line C1A.2.
source: PCR using primers within the chloramphenicol resistance gene (CAT-F and CAT-R) was carried out. A positive control was included using the pAmpChl artificial minicircle. A single product was obtained from lines C1A.1 and C1A.3, with no product detected from line C1A.2 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Sequencing confirmed that products from lines C1A.1 and C1A.3 were the same as expected from pAmpChl.
source: Products from lines C1A.1 and C1A.3 were cloned and sequenced. The sequence was the same as that expected from pAmpChl, which confirmed that the chloramphenicol-resistant A. carterae did indeed contain the pAmpChl sequence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from DNA sequencing.

claim: PCR with primers immediately flanking the psbA gene amplified both psbA and CAT products from pAmpChl-transformed cells.
source: We therefore designed primers immediately flanking the psbA gene (copy-F and copy-R), in a region that was common to both the psbA and pAmpChl minicircles, and carried out PCR. This should amplify either psbA or CAT. Analysis of the products using agarose gel electrophoresis revealed the presence of two bands, one corresponding to the psbA gene and one to the CAT gene, as shown in Figure 3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There are roughly similar numbers of psbA and pAmpChl minicircles in the chloroplast of transformed cells.
source: Taking into account the size of the products, the likelihood that the CAT-specific product would be generated more efficiently, being smaller, and the relative intensity of each band, it would appear that there are roughly similar numbers of each minicircle in the chloroplast.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3 considering PCR product sizes and band intensities.

claim: RT-PCRs using RNA from three atrazine-selected lines in Experiment A6 all yielded a band consistent with the size of the positive control.
source: RT-PCRs using RNA from the three atrazine-selected lines in Experiment A6 all yielded a band consistent with the size of the positive control, Figure 4A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sequencing confirmed that RT-PCR products from all three atrazine-selected lines matched the pAmpPSBA artificial minicircle, confirming that it was transcribed.
source: The DNA in the bands was purified, cloned and sequenced. The sequence of all three matched the pAmpPSBA artificial minicircle, confirming that it was transcribed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR and sequencing.

claim: The RT-PCR sequence spanned the site of the atrazine resistance mutations and included the expected sequence alterations.
source: The sequence spanned the site of the atrazine resistance mutations and included the expected sequence alterations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from sequencing.

claim: RT-PCRs using RNA from two of three chloramphenicol-selected lines in Experiment C3 yielded bands.
source: RT-PCRs using RNA from the three chloramphenicol-selected lines (C3.1-C3.3) yielded bands from two of the three cell lines in Experiment C3 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The RT-PCR products from chloramphenicol-selected lines were sequenced and shown to correspond to the pAmpChl minicircle.
source: The PCR products were sequenced directly and shown to correspond to the pAmpChl minicircle.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR and sequencing.

claim: Immunofluorescence assay with an anti-chloramphenicol acetyl transferase antibody showed that the antibodies co-localized with the chloroplast.
source: In order to confirm that we had transformed the chloroplast genome and not the nuclear genome, we carried out an immunofluorescence assay with an anti-chloramphenicol acetyl transferase antibody, together with a secondary antibody labeled with Alexa Fluor 405. The antibodies co-localized with the chloroplast, identified as the region of the cell with significant autofluorescence, as shown in Figure 5.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The antibodies did not localize with the nucleus or other parts of the cell.
source: The antibodies did not localize with the nucleus or other parts of the cell.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The CAT protein is expressed in the chloroplast.
source: This result shows that the CAT protein is expressed in the chloroplast (compare the merged image with the chloroplast autofluorescence and CAT images).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The pAmpChl artificial minicircle must be located in the chloroplast because the CAT gene did not include a chloroplast targeting sequence.
source: As the CAT gene did not include a chloroplast targeting sequence (which would be necessary to target nuclear-encoded proteins to the chloroplast), the pAmpChl artificial minicircle must be located in the chloroplast.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data and knowledge that nuclear-encoded chloroplast proteins require targeting sequences.

claim: Cells shot with gold particles carrying pAmpPSBA and cultured under continuous atrazine selection at 1 µg ml−1 showed cell count increases over time, although at a rate much lower (~10%) than untransformed cells under no selection.
source: To test if the atrazine-resistance phenotype transformation of the dinoflagellate chloroplast was stable under low-level selection, cells were shot with gold particles carrying pAmpPSBA and cultured under continuous atrazine selection at 1 µg ml−1 (experiment A9 in Table 1). Cell counts increased over time, although at a rate much lower (~10%) than untransformed cells under no selection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cell counting.

claim: After 3 months under low-level atrazine selection, PCR confirmed the presence of pAmpPSBA in three transformed cell lines but not in untransformed cells.
source: After 3 months, cells were harvested and DNA was isolated. PCR using the primers MC-pG-F and MC-pG-R was carried out (as above). A positive control PCR was included using the pAmpPSBA vector, and PCR with DNA isolated from the untransformed, wild type cells maintained at non-lethal atrazine concentration was included as a negative control (Figure 6A). A single product, of expected size, was obtained using the three transformed cell lines, with no product detected from the untransformed cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: DNA sequencing confirmed that the products from all three lines after 3 months corresponded to pAmpPSBA.
source: DNA sequencing confirmed that the products from all three lines corresponded to pAmpPSBA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from DNA sequencing.

claim: The transformation of A. carterae with pAmpPSBA was stable at a non-lethal atrazine concentration.
source: This showed that the transformation of A. carterae with pAmpPSBA was stable at a non-lethal atrazine concentration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing maintenance of the introduced gene over 3 months.

claim: Three lines were generated by shooting with gold particles carrying pAmpChl and cultured under continuous chloramphenicol selection at 20 µg ml−1 with subculturing every 14 days.
source: To test if the chloramphenicol-resistance phenotype transformation of the dinoflagellate chloroplast was stable, three lines were generated by shooting with gold particles carrying pAmpChl and cultured under continuous chloramphenicol selection at 20 µg ml−1 (Experiment C4 in Table 2) with subculturing every 14 days.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: After 18 weeks, PCR confirmed the presence of pAmpChl in all three transformed lines.
source: After 18 weeks, well after control untransformed cells had died, a sample of cells was harvested from each transformed line and DNA was isolated. A PCR reaction using the primers CAT-F-Nest and CAT-R-Nest was carried out on each sample. A positive control PCR was included using the pAmpChl vector (Figure 6B). A single product, of expected size, was obtained for each of the three transformed cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: DNA sequencing confirmed that the products from all three lines after 18 weeks corresponded to pAmpChl.
source: DNA sequencing confirmed that the products from all three lines corresponded to pAmpChl.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from DNA sequencing.

claim: The cultures remained alive 1 year post-transformation at the time of writing.
source: The cultures remained alive at the time of writing, 1 year post-transformation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation of culture viability.

claim: There was stable transformation of A. carterae with pAmpChl.
source: These results show that there was stable transformation of A. carterae with pAmpChl.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing maintenance of the introduced gene and phenotype over 1 year.

claim: A modified version of an existing sequence as well as a heterologous gene were introduced into the dinoflagellate chloroplast.
source: By making use of the plasmid-like fragmented chloroplast genome and a biolistic system, we have introduced a modified version of an existing sequence as well as a heterologous gene.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing introduction of modified psbA and CAT genes.

claim: The introduced genes are transcribed and produce protein, as shown by immunofluorescence microscopy and the presence of an expected phenotype.
source: These genes are transcribed, and produce protein, as shown by immunofluorescence microscopy and the presence of an expected phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR, immunofluorescence, and survival under selection.

claim: Stable transformation was achieved with two separate artificial minicircles, one containing a modified psbA gene designed to confer atrazine tolerance and another encoding chloramphenicol resistance, with cultures surviving at least 1 year under selection.
source: Stable transformation was achieved with two separate artificial minicircles, one containing a modified psbA gene designed to confer atrazine tolerance and another encoding chloramphenicol resistance, with cultures surviving at least 1 year under selection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing long-term culture survival and maintenance of introduced genes.

claim: The copy number of the artificial minicircle is similar to that of native minicircles.
source: The copy number of the artificial minicircle is similar to that of native minicircles.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 comparing band intensities of psbA and CAT PCR products.

claim: A. carterae cells transformed with the modified psbA gene survived under non-lethal concentrations of atrazine for at least 3 months, retaining the modified gene.
source: A. carterae cells transformed with the modified psbA gene (atrazine tolerance) survived under non-lethal concentrations of atrazine for at least 3 months, retaining the modified gene, indicating that the transformation is stable even under low levels of selection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment A9.

claim: It is important to titrate the concentration of selective agents used.
source: The results suggest it is important to titrate the concentration of selective agents used.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental results showing different survival outcomes at different selective agent concentrations.

claim: With an atrazine concentration of 2.5 μg ml−1 some of the transformed cultures did not survive more than a few days longer than untransformed ones, suggesting that the modified PsbA was at least partially inhibited at that higher atrazine concentration.
source: With an atrazine concentration of 2.5 μg ml−1 some of the transformed cultures did not survive more than a few days longer than untransformed ones, suggesting that the modified PsbA was at least partially inhibited at that higher atrazine concentration.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: It is possible that a background of minicircles containing wild-type psbA genes competed with the introduced artificial minicircles for replication or transcription factors.
source: In addition, it is possible that a background of minicircles containing wild-type psbA genes competed with the introduced artificial minicircles for replication or transcription factors, making it difficult for adequate levels of atrazine-insensitive PsbA to be maintained to cope with the higher atrazine concentration.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed results.

claim: With chloramphenicol concentrations of 30 μg ml−1 or above, the survival of transformed and untransformed strains was similar.
source: With chloramphenicol concentrations of 30 μg ml−1 or above, the survival of transformed and untransformed strains was similar.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: At 20 μg ml−1 or lower chloramphenicol, the transformed cultures outlasted the untransformed ones, and some were able to survive apparently indefinitely.
source: However, at 20 μg ml−1 or lower the transformed cultures outlasted the untransformed ones, and some were able to survive apparently indefinitely.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: The primary reason for failure of the majority of methods to give stable transformation is due to inability of the DNA to enter the cell, rather than inherent dinoflagellate genetics.
source: Our results – using the same artificial minicircle in all experiments – suggest that the primary reason for failure of the majority of methods to give stable transformation is due to inability of the DNA to enter the cell, rather than inherent dinoflagellate genetics.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only biolistics succeeded while other methods failed with the same constructs.

claim: The ability to modify the dinoflagellate chloroplast genome will be of enormous value in many areas of dinoflagellate biology.
source: The ability to modify the dinoflagellate chloroplast genome will be of enormous value in many areas of dinoflagellate biology.
evidence: This is speculation about the future impact of the developed method.

claim: Modification of existing minicircles should allow study of many other aspects of the highly unusual chloroplast genome, such as the promoter regions of the genes.
source: Modification of existing minicircles should allow us to study many other aspects of this highly unusual chloroplast genome, such as the promoter regions of the genes.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications of the method.

claim: Many chloroplast genes are down-regulated under high temperature stress.
source: For example, many chloroplast genes are down-regulated under high temperature stress (Gierz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gierz et al., 2017.

claim: Little is known about how transcription is regulated or initiated in dinoflagellate chloroplasts.
source: Little is known about how transcription is regulated, or initiated (Barbrook et al., 2012), though it is assumed that initiation occurs in the conserved core region of the minicircle (Barbrook et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on knowledge from the literature supported by citations to Barbrook et al., 2012; Barbrook et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2002.

claim: It is assumed that transcription initiation occurs in the conserved core region of the minicircle.
source: Little is known about how transcription is regulated, or initiated (Barbrook et al., 2012), though it is assumed that initiation occurs in the conserved core region of the minicircle (Barbrook et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barbrook et al., 2001 and Zhang et al., 2002.

claim: We do not know how the minicircles are replicated, although it is assumed the core region is important.
source: We also do not know how the minicircles are replicated (Barbrook et al., 2018), although again it is assumed the core region is important.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from the literature supported by citation to Barbrook et al., 2018.

claim: It will now be possible to mutate the core region to determine which sections are important.
source: It will now be possible to mutate this core region to determine which sections are important.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications enabled by the transformation method.

claim: The ability to express heterologous proteins will be of great value in studying a wide range of other aspects of dinoflagellate chloroplast biology.
source: The ability to express heterologous proteins will be of great value in studying a wide range of other aspects of dinoflagellate chloroplast biology.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications of the method.

claim: The ability to express modified forms of the PsbA protein will be of particular value in studying the role of this protein in the response by dinoflagellates to the disturbances that are believed to precipitate coral bleaching.
source: The ability to express modified forms of the PsbA protein will be of particular value in studying the role of this protein in the response by dinoflagellates to the disturbances that are believed to precipitate coral bleaching.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications of the method.
